The [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)) of the United Kingdom is a one of the two major parties in the UK's [two-party political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_United_Kingdom).  Since April 2020, the leader of the Labour Party is [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer).

The House of Commons [states](https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/SN03938/SN03938.pdf) that a leadership election is held if there is a vacancy in that role (such as from a resignation or vote of no confidence), or if the Leader is challenged prior to the annual session of the Party conference.  The incumbent is not required to be nominated and is automatically on the ballot; other candidates must recieve nominations from at least 10% of elected [MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom))s (or at least 20% if the Leader is being challenged).  Candidates are elected by party members with an [instant-runoff system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting).

In June 2022, [The Times](https://archive.ph/t5GyY) reported that Keir Starmer was preparing his colleagues for a new leadership election if he was called to step down (for instance, in response to the ["beergate" scanadal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#Partygate_and_Beergate_controversy)).  The Times named [Wes Streeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Streeting) and [Lisa Nandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Nandy) as likely candidates.

Angela Rayner’s resignation as Labour Party deputy leader and vice‑prime minister has triggered a high‑stakes internal contest to replace her. Rayner stepped down after an independent ministerial interests adviser found she had breached the ministerial code by paying less stamp duty on her Hove flat. Her departure removes a key voice from the government and forces the party to elect a new deputy leader, though the winner will not automatically become deputy prime minister. The contest comes at a fragile moment for Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who had just announced a ‘Phase Two’ restart of his administration. Public opinion is weak: a YouGov tracker in August recorded Starmer at 24 % favourable versus 68 % unfavourable, and a Survation poll last month found 64 % of Labour members believe the party is heading in the wrong direction, with Starmer’s net favourability among members falling to –9. Rayner’s exit could energise left‑wing Labour to push for a deputy leader who represents that flank, mirroring the balance of power in Starmer’s leadership. The National Executive Committee will set a timetable for the election. Under current rules, candidates must secure nominations from 20 % of the 80 Labour MPs (i.e., 16 MPs) and the backing of 5 % of constituency parties plus three affiliates, at least two of which must be trade unions. Once nominations are secured, members and affiliates will vote in a preferential ballot. Potential candidates include Shabana Mahmood, the new Home Secretary and a close ally of Starmer; Ed Miliband, the Energy Secretary and former party leader, who currently enjoys a net rating of +74 in a Labour List poll; Emily Thornberry, chair of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee, who has a strong profile; and Wes Streeting, the Health Secretary, whose net rating is only +9. The contest will decide who will become the next deputy leader of the Labour Party.

summary: All forecasting experts agree that Wes Streeting is a plausible but distinctly unlikely winner of the next UK Labour Party leadership election. There is currently no imminent leadership contest; Keir Starmer remains leader, and Labour’s internal rules and recent general election victory make a near-term vacancy improbable. Across perspectives—ranging from political consulting to political science, sociology, and British studies—Streeting’s prospects are hampered by several key factors: 1) his modest popularity among party members (net favourability +9, far behind rivals like Ed Miliband at +74); 2) the presence of stronger and more popular likely contenders such as Andy Burnham (if he becomes an MP), Shabana Mahmood, and Ed Miliband; 3) his centrist or 'Blairite' positioning, which is not aligned with the current grassroots mood seeking an alternative to Starmer-style leadership; and 4) Labour’s nomination thresholds and instant-runoff system, which favour well-networked, broadly appealing, or factionally dominant candidates. Experts highlight that Streeting’s path relies on a very specific set of circumstances: an unexpected vacancy, rivals being unavailable or divided, and a rapid consolidation of support as a unity or compromise candidate. Although his high profile and connections give him a nonzero chance, all base rate and party mood evidence points to him being an underdog. Final probabilities assigned to Streeting winning the leadership range between 3% and 8%, with the average around 6%.
